The [[Kamo River]] and Takano River join on the Tadasu River Banks (Jp., Tadasu-gawara 糺河原). There is the "River Confluence" shrine of [[Shimogamo Shrine]], leading to the forested area called [[Tadasu no Mori|Tadasu-no-mori]].

'''Takano River''' (高野川, ''Takanogawa'') is a {{jalink|一級水系|Q2908753|一級河川}} of the {{jalink|淀川|Q1140505}} river system flowing through {{jalink|左京区|Q1321832}}, {{jalink|京都市|Q34600}}, {{jalink|京都府|Q120730}}<ref name=18_Takanogawa/>.

== Geography ==
The river originates in the southern part of {{jalink|途中越|Q11639484|途中峠}}, on the border of Sakyō-ku, Kyoto and {{jalink|滋賀県|Q131358}}{{jalink|大津市|Q202907}}<ref name=18_Takanogawa/>. It then flows southward parallel to {{jalink|国道367号|Q405076}}<ref name=Heibon/>. It joins a stream originating from Mitani Pass in the northern part of {{jalink|大原 (京都市)|Q3594017|大原}}, Sakyō-ku at Mitsutaniguchi, and joins '''Takatanigawa''' originating from Amagatake on the border of {{jalink|鞍馬|Q4247779}}, Sakyō-ku and Ōhara, Sakyō-ku at Koideishi-chō<ref name=18_Takanogawa/>. The upper reach is sometimes called '''Ōharagawa''' and the middle reach '''Yasegawa'''<ref name=Heibon/>.

It also joins '''Rokkawa''', originating from the hills behind {{jalink|三千院|Q1072538}}, and '''Kusamugawa''', originating from the hills behind {{jalink|寂光院|Q911985}}, and flows southward along the western foothills of {{jalink|比叡山|Q748040}}<ref name=18_Takanogawa/>. At Hanazono Bridge in Kamitakano it crosses {{jalink|白川通|Q11579747}}, joins first-class rivers '''Iwakuragawa''' and '''{{jalink|音羽川 (京都市)|Q30931091|音羽川}}''', runs alongside {{jalink|川端通|Q11055642}}, and merges with first-class river '''{{jalink|鴨川 (京都府)|Q27218|鴨川}}''' upstream of Kamo Ōbashi<ref name=18_Takanogawa/>. On maps of Kyoto, the Kamo River is often depicted as a Y-shape; the Takano River forms the right branch<ref name=18_Takanogawa/>.

== Wildlife ==
[[File:Cervus nippon passing Takano river 20160713.jpg|thumb|left|250px|A Japanese deer family crossing the Takano River]]
* {{jalink|オオサンショウウオ|Q112045}} - {{jalink|特別天然記念物|Q96207459}} Japanese giant salamanders inhabit the river. After heavy rains, they are occasionally carried downstream to central Kyoto, surprising residents<ref name=sankei20150723/>.
* {{jalink|ニホンジカ|Q190516}} - Japanese deer can sometimes be seen on the riverbanks<ref name=asahi20101111/>.

== History ==
Currently, the Kamogawa flows from the northwest and joins the Takano River near Demachiyanagi before flowing south as the Kamo River. However, it was formerly believed that the Kamogawa flowed south from near Kamigamo while the Takano River flowed southwest from near Demachiyanagi, with both rivers forming alluvial fans across the Sakyō area (Tsukamoto Tsuneo, "{{jalink|鴨川 (京都府)#鴨川つけかえ説|Q27218|鴨川つけかえ説}}"<ref>Tsukamoto Tsuneo, "Historical Changes in Kyoto City and Their Geographical Analysis," 1931, ''Chirigironso'' Vol. 1.</ref>). Geological research has proposed that during the {{jalink|最終氷期|Q754949}} the rivers merged with the Kamo River at a point further south than in later periods<ref>Yokoyama Takuo, ''Heian Relocation and the Kamogawa Course Change'', 1988, Hosei Publishers</ref>. For a time, many historians followed this theory and concluded that "there was no course change," but more recently voices calling for a reassessment of the "course change theory" have grown<ref>Takahashi Manabu, "Flood Damage of Kyoto's Kamo and Katsura Rivers in the Early Modern Period," 2012, ''Kyoto's Historical Disasters'', Shibunkaku; Kotani Shinjiró, ''Water-Viewed Kyoto: History and Daily Life of Urban Formation'', 2007, Hosei University Eco Regional Design Research Institute; Uemura Yoshihiro, ''Kyoto's Flood Control and the Shōwa Great Flood'', 2011, Bunrikaku</ref>.
According to the "{{jalink|日本後紀|Q1077029}}", the Takano River was called '''Hanigawa''' during the Heian period<ref name=18_Takanogawa/>. According to the "{{jalink|雍州府志|Q18460389}}", the river's name derives from flowing through Takano Village<ref name=18_Takanogawa/>.

The river has long been prized as agricultural water, with surrounding villages benefiting from it, though inter-village conflicts arose repeatedly during droughts<ref name=Heibon/>. As of September {{jalink|2019年|Q25274}} ({{jalink|令和|Q62609017}} Year 1), part of the Ōhara area still uses it as a drinking water source<ref name=Kyoto20170401/><ref name=Kyoto20190927/>.

== Major tributaries ==
[[File:Confluence of Iwakura and Takano rivers 20200512.jpg|thumb|200px|Confluence of the Takano River (right) and Iwakura River (left) between Hanazono Bridge and Yamabana Bridge]]
The main tributaries flowing into the Takano River are as follows<ref name=18_Takanogawa/><ref name=Seibi/>:
* 高谷川
* 呂川
** 律川
* 草生川
* 岩倉川
* 音羽川
{{-}}
=== Distributaries ===
* 泉川 (Izumigawa)
: Branching from the Takano River at Yamabana, Matsugasaki, Sakyō-ku, the Izumigawa flows through Matsugasaki while diverting agricultural water along the way, crosses the {{jalink|琵琶湖疏水|Q2753954}} branch canal at {{jalink|下鴨|Q11361517}}<ref name=Gakku/>, flows through the grounds of Shimogamo Shrine ({{jalink|賀茂御祖神社|Q701620}}), and then rejoins the Takano River<ref name=izumigawa/>.

== Major bridges ==
[[File:Eiden 901 over Takano river bridge 2020-05-04.jpg|thumb|right|Takano River (from Hanazono Bridge)]]
(South of Yase Dam)
河原人道橋 - 三宅橋 - 花園橋 - 山端橋 - 松ヶ崎橋 - 馬橋 - 高野川北泉橋 - 松ヶ崎人道橋 - 高野橋 - 蓼倉（たでくら）橋 - 御蔭橋 - 河合橋<ref name=map1/><ref name=bridge1/>

== Regulatory restrictions ==
Under the {{jalink|京都府鴨川条例|Q11375572}} (enacted April {{jalink|2008年|Q2004}}), the section south of Mabashi on the Takano River, along with sections south of the Kamogawa Takahashi Bridge and north of the Kamogawa Kyoto Minami Ōhashi, are subject to regulation, restricting activities such as launching fireworks<ref name=Jorei/>.
